content: ATPase inhibitor, mitochondrial, is an enzyme encoded by the ATPIF1 gene in humans. This gene produces a mitochondrial ATPase inhibitor. Alternative splicing occurs at this gene locus, resulting in three transcript variants that encode distinct isoforms. The primary function of this inhibitor is to prevent ATPase from switching to ATP hydrolysis when the electrochemical gradient collapses, such as during oxygen deprivation. The ATP synthase inhibitor forms a one-to-one complex with the F1 ATPase, potentially by binding at the interface between the alpha and beta subunits. It is believed to inhibit ATP synthesis by preventing the release of ATP. The inhibitor exists in two oligomeric states: a dimer, which is the active state, and a tetramer. At low pH, the inhibitor forms a dimer through antiparallel coiled-coil interactions between the C-terminal regions of two monomers. At high pH, the inhibitor assembles into tetramers and higher-order oligomers via coiled-coil interactions involving the N-terminal region and the inhibitory domain, which suppresses its inhibitory activity. Model organisms have been utilized to study the function of ATPIF1. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Atpif1tm1a(EUCOMM)Wtsi, was created as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program. This program is a high-throughput mutagenesis initiative designed to generate and distribute animal models of human diseases to researchers. Male and female mice from this line underwent a standardized phenotypic screening to assess the effects of ATPIF1 deletion. A total of 23 tests were conducted on the mutant mice, and three significant abnormalities were identified. Homozygous mutant mice exhibited hyperactivity and brain dysmorphology. Additionally, male mice showed reduced levels of circulating alkaline phosphatase.
